title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, decide whether every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket in the correct nesting order.

nearMiss.why: Matching from both ends fails for '()[]': brackets close the most recent opener, not the opposite end.
Counting each bracket type ignores order: '([)]' has equal counts but is invalid.
Nothing is kept in sorted order; the stack mirrors nesting.

trigger.why: Nesting ⇒ the most recently opened must close first ⇒ LIFO stack.

ds.why: ArrayDeque push/pop/peek; avoid the legacy Stack class.

invariant.answer: The stack holds exactly the currently unclosed openers, innermost on top.
wrong: The stack is always empty after a closing bracket.
The stack holds closing brackets waiting for openers.
The stack size equals the string length at every step.
invariant.why: A closer must match the top; at the end the stack must be empty.

space.why: All openers in the worst case.

wrong: Two pointers need the string sorted.
Two pointers only work on even-length strings.

approach: Push openers; on a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener (pop). Valid iff the stack ends empty.

title: Decode String
statement: Decode an encoded string where k[text] means text repeated k times, and brackets can be nested, e.g. 3[a2[c]] → accaccacc.

nearMiss.why: The repeated text isn't a window with a property; it's a nested structure.
There are no choices to explore; the decoding is deterministic.
No overlapping subproblems over prefixes; the difficulty is nesting, not optimisation.

trigger.why: Nested brackets ⇒ save the outer context when you enter '[' and restore it at ']' ⇒ stack (or recursion).

ds.answer: Two stacks: ArrayDeque<Integer> counts and ArrayDeque<StringBuilder> partial strings
ds.why: Each '[' pushes (count, string so far); each ']' pops and appends the repeated current string.

invariant.answer: The stacks hold, for every open '[', the repeat count and the text built before it; current holds the text inside the innermost open bracket.
wrong: The stacks are empty whenever a letter is read.
current always holds the final decoded string.
Counts are popped when a digit is read.
invariant.why: That is exactly the context needed to resume after ']'.

wrong: O(n²) in the input length only
time.why: Every output character is written (and copied a bounded number of times per level).

space.why: The partial strings on the stack plus the result.

wrong: Sliding window needs the string sorted.
Sliding window only works with one bracket pair.

approach: Scan: digits build k; '[' pushes k and current, then resets both; ']' pops prev and k and sets current = prev + current × k; letters append to current.

title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string of lowercase letters and '(' and ')', remove the minimum number of parentheses so that the result is valid, and return any valid result.

nearMiss.why: Trying all removal subsets is exponential; one pass with a stack finds exactly which to drop.
Dropping unmatched ')' greedily is right, but unmatched '(' are only known at the end; the stack remembers their positions.
No interval optimisation is needed; matching is decided in one scan.

trigger.answer: remove the minimum number of parentheses
trigger.why: Matching parentheses ⇒ stack of unmatched '(' indices; any ')' with an empty stack and any leftover '(' must go.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices of unmatched '(' plus a boolean[] (or Set) of indices to delete
ds.why: A single counter can't tell you WHICH '(' were unmatched.

invariant.answer: The stack holds indices of '(' not yet matched; every ')' seen with an empty stack is marked for removal.
wrong: The stack holds indices of ')' characters.
The balance counter never goes negative.
Letters are pushed onto the stack too.
invariant.why: After the scan, leftover stack indices plus marked ')' are exactly the minimum removals.

space.why: Stack, marks and the output builder.

wrong: Backtracking only works on strings without letters.
Backtracking always returns the empty string.

approach: Scan: push index of '('; on ')' pop if possible, else mark it. Mark all indices left on the stack. Build the string skipping marked indices.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: Given daily temperatures, return for each day how many days you have to wait until a warmer temperature. Use 0 if there is no future warmer day.

nearMiss.why: Scanning forward from each day is O(n²); the stack resolves all waiting days in one pass.
A heap orders by temperature but loses the 'first warmer day after me' relation to position.
There is no fixed window to expire from the front; elements wait until resolved.

wrong: how many days you have to wait
Use 0 if there is no future warmer day
trigger.why: 'Next greater element' for every position ⇒ monotonic stack of unresolved indices.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with decreasing temperatures
wrong: int[] next-warmer table filled by two loops
ds.why: Indices give distances; decreasing values keep unresolved days on top.

invariant.answer: Indices on the stack haven't found a warmer day yet, and their temperatures decrease from bottom to top.
wrong: The stack is always sorted increasing from bottom to top.
The stack holds every index seen so far.
The top of the stack is always the warmest day.
invariant.why: A warmer day pops every cooler day it resolves.

time.why: Each index pushed and popped once.

space.why: The stack in a strictly decreasing run.

wrong: Two pointers need the temperatures sorted.
Two pointers would use O(n²) memory.

approach: For each i: while the stack top is cooler than temps[i], pop j and set answer[j] = i − j; push i.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Given bar heights of a histogram (each bar width 1), return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.

nearMiss.why: Shrinking from both ends (like Container With Most Water) fails: the rectangle's height is the minimum over the whole span, not just the ends.
No simple recurrence; what you need per bar is the nearest smaller bar on each side.
There's no validity rule that monotonically breaks as the window grows.

trigger.answer: largest rectangle that fits entirely inside
trigger.why: For each bar, the widest rectangle at its height spans to the nearest SMALLER bar on each side ⇒ monotonic stack.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with increasing heights, plus a sentinel 0 at the end
wrong: int[][] min-height table for every span
ds.why: When a bar is popped, the new top is its left boundary and the current index its right boundary.

invariant.answer: Heights on the stack increase from bottom to top; a bar is popped exactly when its right boundary (first smaller bar) is found.
wrong: Heights on the stack decrease from bottom to top.
The stack always holds the tallest bar seen.
Each bar's rectangle ends at the last index.
invariant.why: At pop time both boundaries are known, so area = height × (i − newTop − 1).

time.why: Each index pushed and popped once.

wrong: Two pointers need the heights sorted.
Two pointers only work on even numbers of bars.

approach: Append height 0. For each i: while heights[top] > heights[i], pop h; width = stack empty ? i : i − newTop − 1; best = max(best, h × width). Push i.

title: Basic Calculator II
statement: Evaluate a string expression of non-negative integers, spaces and the operators + - * / (integer division truncating toward zero), with no parentheses. Multiplication and division bind tighter than addition and subtraction. Don't use a built-in eval.

nearMiss.why: Nothing is kept in sorted order; the stack holds pending signed terms to add at the end.
Building an expression tree works but is overkill without parentheses; one pass with a stack of terms suffices.
Scanning with indices finds tokens, but precedence needs somewhere to hold the pending + / − terms.

trigger.answer: bind tighter than addition and subtraction
trigger.why: Operator precedence ⇒ defer + / − terms on a stack, apply * / immediately to the top.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack of signed terms (or a running sum + last term)
ds.why: The O(1)-space variant keeps 'sum so far' and 'last term' instead of the stack.

invariant.answer: The stack holds fully evaluated additive terms; the answer is their sum. When the previous operator is * or /, the top term is updated in place.
wrong: The stack always holds exactly two numbers.
Operators are pushed in increasing precedence.
The top of the stack is the final answer at every step.
invariant.why: − pushes −num; * and / combine with the top; + pushes num.

space.why: Up to one term per number.

wrong: A monotonic stack can't hold negative terms.
Monotonic stacks only work with parentheses.
A monotonic stack would evaluate right to left.

approach: Parse num; on an operator (or end) apply the PREVIOUS op: + push num, − push −num, * push pop()·num, / push pop()/num. Sum the stack.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: Given tokens of an arithmetic expression in postfix order (each operator follows its two operands), evaluate it. Operators are + - * / and division truncates toward zero.

nearMiss.why: You could build the expression tree and evaluate it recursively, but postfix order is already the evaluation order for a stack.
There's no ordering property to maintain; operands are pushed and popped as operators arrive.
No subproblems overlap; each token is used exactly once.

trigger.answer: each operator follows its two operands
trigger.why: Postfix ⇒ push operands, and each operator pops two and pushes the result.

wrong: int[] of operands indexed by position

invariant.answer: The stack holds the values of all complete sub-expressions not yet consumed; a valid expression ends with exactly one value.
wrong: The stack size grows by one per token.
The top is always the largest operand.
invariant.why: Pop b then a, push a op b (order matters for − and /).

wrong: Tree DFS would evaluate operators before operands.
A tree would need the tokens sorted.

approach: For each token: if operator, b = pop, a = pop, push(a op b); else push(parseInt). Return pop().

title: Asteroid Collision
statement: Asteroids in a row move right if positive and left if negative, with size |value|. When a right-mover meets a left-mover, the smaller explodes (both if equal). Return the asteroids that remain after all collisions.

nearMiss.why: Collisions cascade: a big left-mover can destroy several earlier right-movers, so you need everything unresolved behind you, not just two indices.
Pops happen because of a collision rule, not to keep values sorted; the surviving stack isn't monotonic in size.
There's no choice to make; the physics decides. The question is how to replay it efficiently.

trigger.answer: When a right-mover meets a left-mover
trigger.why: The newest item interacts with the most recent unresolved ones ⇒ a stack.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> as a stack of survivors
ds.why: Read survivors bottom to top at the end.

invariant.answer: The stack holds survivors so far, and no collision is pending among them (no right-mover directly below a left-mover).
wrong: The stack is sorted by size.
Every asteroid is pushed exactly once and never popped.
invariant.why: A new left-mover pops smaller right-movers until it dies or nothing can hit it.

time.why: Each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once.

wrong: Two pointers can't handle negative values.
Two pointers would need the asteroids sorted by size.
Two pointers only work when all asteroids move the same way.

approach: For a: while a < 0 and top > 0: if top < −a pop and continue; if top == −a pop and a dies; else a dies. If a survives push it.

title: Next Greater Element II
statement: Given a circular integer array (after the last element comes the first), return for every element the first strictly larger value found by walking forward, or -1 if none exists.

nearMiss.why: A plain stack isn't enough: the key is keeping it DECREASING so each pop answers a waiting element.
Scanning forward per element is O(n²).
Nothing expires from the front: there's no window, just pending elements waiting for a bigger value.

trigger.answer: the first strictly larger value found by walking forward
trigger.why: 'Next greater' ⇒ monotonic stack; circular ⇒ iterate 2n indices using i % n.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of indices with decreasing values, plus int[] result filled with -1
wrong: int[] doubled copy of the array
ds.why: Indices let you write the answer when popped; i % n avoids copying.

invariant.answer: The stack holds indices still waiting for a greater value, with values strictly decreasing from bottom to top.
wrong: The stack holds the k largest values seen.
Values increase from bottom to top.
invariant.why: Only push during the first pass (i < n); the second pass only pops.

time.why: Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

wrong: A plain stack can't store indices.
Stacks don't work on circular arrays.
A plain stack would find the previous greater instead.

approach: For i in 0..2n−1: x = nums[i % n]; while stack non-empty and nums[top] < x, result[pop] = x; if i < n push i.

title: Online Stock Span
statement: Design a class that receives one daily stock price at a time. For each new price, return its span: the number of consecutive days ending today (including today) whose price was less than or equal to today's.

nearMiss.why: It is a class, but the whole trick is one monotonic stack; there's nothing to combine.
The window length isn't fixed or budgeted; it reaches back to the previous greater price.
Prices aren't sorted, so you can't binary-search for the previous greater one.

wrong: one daily stock price at a time
less than or equal to today's
trigger.why: Span = distance to the previous GREATER element ⇒ monotonic stack, folding the spans of popped days into the new one.

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<int[]> of (price, span) with strictly decreasing prices
wrong: ArrayList<Integer> of all prices, scanned back
ds.why: Storing the span lets you skip the popped days without keeping them.

invariant.answer: Prices on the stack strictly decrease from bottom to top, and each entry's span covers the days it absorbed.
wrong: The stack holds every price seen.
Spans on the stack are increasing.
The top is always yesterday's price.
invariant.why: Popped days can never be the 'previous greater' for any later day.

time.why: Each price is pushed and popped once in total.

wrong: A design problem would need a database.
Design classes must use a HashMap.

approach: span = 1; while top.price ≤ price: span += pop().span; push(price, span); return span.

title: Remove K Digits
statement: Given a non-negative integer as a string and an integer k, remove exactly k digits so that the remaining number is the smallest possible. Return it as a string without leading zeros ("0" if empty).

nearMiss.why: Trying every set of k removals is combinatorial.
No overlapping subproblems are needed: a local rule (drop a digit bigger than its successor) is always safe.
Removing the k largest digits is wrong: position matters more than size ("1432219", k=3 → "1219").

trigger.answer: the remaining number is the smallest possible
wrong: a non-negative integer as a string
trigger.why: Smallest result after deletions ⇒ keep digits non-decreasing from the left: pop a larger previous digit while removals remain.

ds.answer: StringBuilder or ArrayDeque<Character> used as a non-decreasing stack
ds.why: A StringBuilder doubles as the stack and the output.

invariant.answer: The kept digits are non-decreasing; a digit is popped only if a smaller one follows it and removals remain.
wrong: Exactly one digit is removed per step.
The first digit is never removed.
invariant.why: Leftover k: trim from the end; then strip leading zeros.

time.why: Each digit pushed and popped at most once.

wrong: Backtracking would only remove one digit.

approach: For each digit d: while k > 0 and top > d: pop, k−−. push d. Remove k more from the end, strip leading zeros, return "0" if empty.
